Marcus, Doug —

Both finalists finished final-round loops this week. Panel notes attached... actually I'll just summarize here since the scorecard tool is still syncing.

Dr. Renee Castillo (currently AVP Clinical Ops at a 400-bed system in Phoenix) — strong on strategic vision, multi-site scaling experience, weaker on day-to-day staffing operations per two panelists.

subject: Re: VP Clinical Operations (West) — final round debrief
snippet: Tim, Marcus — Here's my full scorecard from both onsite loops, since I know Priya — sorry, Priscilla — wants the detail before she weighs in. Dr. Renee Castillo — Strategy & Vision
body_text:
Tim, Marcus —

Here's my full scorecard from both onsite loops, since I know Priya — sorry, Priscilla — wants the detail before she weighs in.

Dr. Renee Castillo — Strategy & Vision: 4.7/5. She walked through how she took her current system from two regional clinics to eleven in under three years, including the change-management pain points, which is exactly the phase we're entering with the West expansion. On the operations side she was noticeably thinner — when I pressed her on how she'd handle a night-shift staffing shortfall at a single site, she gave a fairly generic answer about escalation paths rather than specifics. Culture fit: good energy, direct communicator, a little polished for my taste but that's a minor note. References were strong — her CNO called her 'the reason our expansion didn't fall apart.'

Anthony Vogel — Strategy & Vision: 3.6/5. Solid but not visionary; he thinks in terms of the next two quarters, not the next three years, which is fair given his current scope. Operations: 4.9/5 — the best operational interview I've sat in this year. He walked the panel through an actual staffing crisis at Aurora last winter, the exact levers he pulled, and the follow-up process changes. He knows our EHR quirks, our union contract nuances, and half the nursing leads by name already. Culture fit: excellent, obviously, he's been here four years.

My honest read: if we're hiring for the next 18 months of just running the region well, it's Anthony, no contest. If we're hiring for the next five years of scaling into new markets, Castillo has a higher ceiling but real ramp risk. I don't think this is a slam dunk either way and I'd rather we argue it out before we make an offer than regret it in six months.

One more data point that didn't fit neatly into a score: I asked both of them the same closing question — 'what would you do in your first 30 days?' Castillo talked almost entirely about stakeholder mapping, a listening tour across the new sites, and a 90-day strategic plan she'd present to Elaine and the board. All reasonable, but it's the answer of someone who's done this at a company with a much bigger management layer underneath her, where thirty days of listening doesn't leave anything on fire. Anthony's answer was narrower and more tactical — shadow the highest-turnover unit for a week, fix the two scheduling bottlenecks he already knows about from his current seat, then start the conversation about the new sites. Neither answer is wrong, but they tell you which job each of them thinks they're walking into, and I'm not convinced either of them has fully absorbed that this role is genuinely both.

Curious to hear Priscilla's read from the nursing leadership panel before we go further.

Doug Feinstein
VP, Clinical Operations
Vireo Health Systems

body_text:
I've sat with this for a week and I want to override, and I want to be straight with all of you about why rather than just pull rank.

Anthony is the safer choice and probably the more popular one on the floor, and if this were a backfill of Doug's role I'd sign off on the committee's vote without a second thought. But it isn't. The board approved this headcount specifically for the West region build-out, and Tomás — sorry, wrong board, I mean our own board — approved it on the premise that we'd bring in someone who has actually built a multi-site region from scratch, not someone who is excellent at running the one we already have. Anthony would be set up to fail at the actual mandate of this job even though he'd be great at the job we already have him doing.

I also don't think this has to be a binary loss for Anthony. I'd like Tim and Doug to talk to him this week about a Senior Director, Clinical Operations role overseeing the existing region directly under whoever we hire — a real promotion, a comp bump, and a much lower-risk on-ramp to the regional VP seat in 18-24 months if that's still what he wants. I don't want to lose him over this.

I know this contradicts where we landed as a group last week and I don't take that lightly. But I'd rather eat the awkwardness of overriding now than the cost of getting the West build-out wrong. Extending the offer to Dr. Castillo — Tim, can you get that moving today? And someone needs to have the Anthony conversation before he hears about the offer secondhand.

CEO, Vireo Health Systems

subject: Re: Night/weekend shift differential — proposal
snippet: Ran both scenarios against current headcount and the open reqs Priscilla flagged. Full model attached, but here's the summary. FTE-only scope (benefits-eligible night/weekend nursi
body_text:
Ran both scenarios against current headcount and the open reqs Priscilla flagged. Full model attached, but here's the summary.

FTE-only scope (benefits-eligible night/weekend nursing staff): annualized cost of the proposal is about $284,000 above current differential spend, based on 96 FTEs currently working qualifying shifts. That's a real number but it's inside the nursing labor variance we're already tracking against budget this year, mostly because we've been running those three reqs open and backfilling with agency staff at a much higher effective rate — agency nurses on nights are running us close to $95/hr loaded versus roughly $58/hr loaded for a differential-adjusted staff RN. So there's a real argument this pays for itself if it closes even two of the three open reqs within two quarters.

FTE+PRN scope: adds another $61,000 annualized for the roughly 22 PRN nurses who pick up qualifying shifts regularly. Smaller number than I expected, honestly, because PRN utilization on nights specifically is lower than I assumed going in.

My recommendation, purely from a numbers standpoint: include PRN. The incremental cost is modest relative to the FTE base cost, and excluding PRN creates an obvious incentive problem — PRN staff would have every reason to decline night/weekend shifts once FTEs are getting paid more for the same work, which undermines exactly the flexibility PRN is supposed to give us.

One flag for budget planning purposes: this isn't currently in the FY26 labor budget as modeled in January, so if approved it needs a formal budget line adjustment, not just a payroll config change. I can draft that adjustment once you have a final scope and effective date. Happy to walk through the model live if useful.

Lena Cho
Senior Financial Analyst, Vireo Health Systems

subject: Re: Accommodation request — coordination needed
snippet: Happy to help get this on rails. Here's the process I'd recommend, at a high level. First, keep the leave determination and the accommodation determination conceptually separate ev
body_text:
Happy to help get this on rails. Here's the process I'd recommend, at a high level.

First, keep the leave determination and the accommodation determination conceptually separate even though they involve the same employee. The leave piece is largely mechanical once you have a certification — confirm FMLA eligibility (12 months of service, 1,250 hours, which given a 200-person employer you're almost certainly covered for), get the medical certification form back within the standard window, and track the leave against the 12-week allotment the normal way. Nothing unusual there procedurally.

The accommodation piece is where I want you to slow down. Once the employee is cleared to return with restrictions, that triggers the ADA interactive process independent of the FMLA leave tracking. That means: get the specific functional restrictions in writing from the treating provider (not a diagnosis — just what tasks are and aren't restricted, for how long), have a real conversation with the employee about what accommodations they believe would work, and separately have the department head assess what's operationally feasible in that role. Document each of those three inputs separately, because if this ever gets scrutinized the thing regulators and plaintiffs' counsel look for first is whether the employer actually engaged in a good-faith, documented back-and-forth rather than just approving or denying unilaterally.

On workers' comp: only relevant if any portion of the underlying condition is claimed to be work-related. If the employee hasn't filed a claim, don't volunteer that theory — but if it comes up, loop in Gail at Fairhaven immediately since that triggers separate reporting obligations.

A couple of process notes that will save you headaches later. First, whatever accommodation you land on, put an end date or a re-evaluation date on it even if the restriction letter doesn't specify one — open-ended accommodations are the single most common thing I see turn into a dispute eighteen months later, because nobody remembers to revisit them and then it looks like either an informal permanent change to the role or, worse, like you forgot the employee existed. Second, if the department head's operational-feasibility assessment concludes something isn't workable, get that in writing too, with the specific operational reason, not just 'doesn't work for the team' — vague denials are what get second-guessed later, specific ones generally hold up fine. Third, resist the urge to solve this entirely over email once the paperwork starts moving; a short call with the employee to walk through the plan tends to land better than a written offer appearing out of nowhere, even when the substance is identical.

Practically: Claudia, get the certification and restriction paperwork moving. Once you have the functional restrictions in hand, send them to me before you propose anything to the employee — I want to sanity-check the proposed accommodation against the restrictions before it's offered, not after. Should be a quick turnaround on my end, typically 24-48 hours.

Happy to get on a call if a conversation would be faster than email for any of this.

Josh Lieberman
Bramwell LLP | Employment Counsel
(303) 555-0166

First, keep the leave determination and the accommodation determination conceptually separate even though they involve the same employee. The leave piece is largely mechanical once you have a certification — confirm FMLA eligibility (12 months of service, 1,250 hours, which given a 200-person employer you're almost certainly covered for), get the medical certification form back within the standard window, and track the leave against the 12-week allotment the normal way. Nothing unusual there procedurally.

The accommodation piece is where I want you to slow down. Once the employee is cleared to return with restrictions, that triggers the ADA interactive process independent of the FMLA leave tracking. That means: get the specific functional restrictions in writing from the treating provider (not a diagnosis — just what tasks are and aren't restricted, for how long), have a real conversation with the employee about what accommodations they believe would work, and separately have the department head assess what's operationally feasible in that role. Document each of those three inputs separately, because if this ever gets scrutinized the thing regulators and plaintiffs' counsel look for first is whether the employer actually engaged in a good-faith, documented back-and-forth rather than just approving or denying unilaterally.

On workers' comp: only relevant if any portion of the underlying condition is claimed to be work-related. If the employee hasn't filed a claim, don't volunteer that theory — but if it comes up, loop in Gail at Fairhaven immediately since that triggers separate reporting obligations.

A couple of process notes that will save you headaches later. First, whatever accommodation you land on, put an end date or a re-evaluation date on it even if the restriction letter doesn't specify one — open-ended accommodations are the single most common thing I see turn into a dispute eighteen months later, because nobody remembers to revisit them and then it looks like either an informal permanent change to the role or, worse, like you forgot the employee existed. Second, if the department head's operational-feasibility assessment concludes something isn't workable, get that in writing too, with the specific operational reason, not just 'doesn't work for the team' — vague denials are what get second-guessed later, specific ones generally hold up fine. Third, resist the urge to solve this entirely over email once the paperwork starts moving; a short call with the employee to walk through the plan tends to land better than a written offer appearing out of nowhere, even when the substance is identical.

Practically: Claudia, get the certification and restriction paperwork moving. Once you have the functional restrictions in hand, send them to me before you propose anything to the employee — I want to sanity-check the proposed accommodation against the restrictions before it's offered, not after. Should be a quick turnaround on my end, typically 24-48 hours.

Happy to get on a call if a conversation would be faster than email for any of this.

subject: Re: Regional Nurse Manager offer — Danielle Ruiz countered
snippet: I'm inclined to approve this, but let me actually walk through my reasoning rather than just say yes, since the sign-on pool is one of the line items the board asked us to hold the
body_text:
I'm inclined to approve this, but let me actually walk through my reasoning rather than just say yes, since the sign-on pool is one of the line items the board asked us to hold the line on this year.

Danielle is exactly the profile we struggle to hire for — a nurse manager with real turnaround experience, not just tenure. Priscilla doesn't oversell candidates lightly, and the fact that she's pushing this hard tells me something. Losing her to a competing offer over a $3,000 gap on a role we've had open for four months would be a bad trade against basically any reasonable measure of cost. The PTO exception doesn't concern me at all — that's squarely a manager-discretion call and exactly the kind of thing I want Marcus and Priscilla deciding without escalating to me.

The sign-on number is where I want to be careful, not because $2,500 is a large sum in isolation, but because of precedent — if this gets discussed among other nurse managers, and it will, I want us to be able to defend it as a genuine market-driven exception rather than something that looks arbitrary. So here's what I'd like: if Finance confirms the sign-on bonus pool has room this quarter without pulling from a line we need elsewhere, approve up to $7,500 — splitting the difference rather than giving her the full $8,000 ask, framed to her as 'we moved as far as we could on sign-on and gave you everything you asked for on PTO and start date.' If Finance says the pool is tight, come back to me and we'll figure out a non-cash sweetener instead — extra CME budget, a later performance review date for her first raise eligibility, something along those lines.

One more thing while I have you both: I'd like recruiting to start tracking counter-negotiation patterns across the nurse manager and director-level reqs specifically, separate from our normal offer-acceptance metrics. My sense, and it's only a sense right now, is that we're seeing more candidates counter on sign-on and PTO than we did eighteen months ago, which either means our base offers have quietly fallen behind market or it means candidates have gotten more sophisticated about negotiating, or both. If it's the former I'd rather fix the base-offer numbers proactively than keep granting one-off exceptions that are individually defensible but collectively look like we don't know what the role is worth. Tim, can you pull the last six months of nurse-manager-and-above offers and flag which ones needed an exception like this one, and roughly how big? Doesn't need to be formal, just want a gut check before comp planning season.

Let's not lose her over $2,500 either way, but let's do it in a way we can defend later.

Elaine Ford, MD
CEO, Vireo Health Systems
